You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Samsung profit surges 19 times but triggers a circuit breaker: "Sell the news" trend erupts among Asian chip stocks!

TEXT:
Source: Jinse Finance
On Tuesday, Asian technology stocks tumbled sharply as investors took advantage of Samsung Electronics Co.'s earnings report to lock in profits after a remarkable year-to-date rally in chip stocks, rotating funds into previously unattractive sectors that are cheaper in valuation and less vulnerable to earnings shocks.
The world's largest memory chip manufacturer posted a quarterly profit surge of 19 times, driven by strong AI demand, but it was only 6% above analyst expectations. Its stock price plummeted as much as 7.9% in Seoul, dragging down peers such as SK Hynix Inc. and Japan's Kioxia Holdings Corp. The MSCI technology stocks index fell as much as 2.7%, while financial and consumer stocks recorded gains.
Korea's benchmark Kospi index dropped more than 6% during the session. The Korea Exchange triggered the Kospi circuit breaker mechanism as Kospi 200 futures fell over 5%, suspending program trading for five minutes.
US stock index futures also dipped slightly during the Asian session. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index contract fell 0.7%, indicating that Monday's rebound on Wall Street might be short-lived.
These market moves provide further evidence that after a significant rally, investors are increasingly skeptical of the AI frenzy. Mainstream headlines in recent years about capacity expansion, technology delays, and rising debt levels—news that once attracted little attention—are now seen as reasons to sell technology stocks.
KCM Trade Chief Market Analyst Tim Waterer said, “Today’s session is the classic ‘sell the fact’ logic—investors have already priced in extremely high expectations. When valuations are stretched and rotation is in full swing, even strong earnings are not enough to satisfy the market.”
Memory chip stocks are among the hottest trades this year, with Kioxia's staggering 600% surge topping Bloomberg 's list of tracked Asian chip manufacturers . Despite the sharp rise in demand, the market is still in wait-and-see mode: will this boom end in a typical bust, or is AI creating a longer-lasting “super cycle”?
Albert Yong, Managing Partner at hedge fund Petra Capital Management, said Samsung's results “enhanced market confidence in the sustained growth of AI-related demand, the resilience of memory prices, and the favorable medium- to long-term outlook for the industry.” However, he also pointed out, “Investors may have anticipated these strong results in advance and will increasingly focus on the longer-term trends of the memory cycle.”
According to Samsung Electronics’ report, preliminary operating profit for the three months ending in June was 89.4 trillion won (about $58 billion), roughly 6% above expectations. Revenue more than doubled to 171 trillion won.
This profit level even exceeded Nvidia’s last quarter operating profit of $53.536 billion, making Samsung Electronics the world’s most profitable company by operating income for the quarter. The company said it will release its full financial report on July 30, which will include details on net profit and business segment breakdowns.
Samsung’s results drew widespread attention, but analysts noted that despite the strong performance of the memory chip business, there are still structural pressures within the company. Losses in the foundry and logic chip (LSI) businesses are expected to widen this quarter, partly because bonus costs are included in the overall costs of the semiconductor division.
This cost change stems from a compensation arrangement reached in May this year. Samsung agreed with its chip division employees to link performance bonuses to operating profit, extracting 10.5% of the full-year semiconductor division operating profit as special bonuses after meeting certain profit criteria. Some analysts believe that excluding this expense, the current quarter’s operating profit would be even higher.
Brian Cho, portfolio manager at Causeway Capital Management, said: “We will look for signs to determine whether this represents a sustainable leap in the company's annual free cash flow generation.” He added that he will also pay attention to management’s performance on shareholder return policies.
According to market research firm Counterpoint, the average operating profit margin of the three major chipmakers is expected to be around 75% to 80% in the June quarter. In a report, Counterpoint said that such high margins could trigger concerns about “excessive profiteering” by memory manufacturers, and if maintained, could invite regulatory scrutiny.
Counterpoint Director Tom Kang said, “I don’t think the market fully realizes how outstanding these figures are.” He noted that the price surge for memory chips was even steeper at the end of the second quarter than at the start. “This boom will certainly continue for the coming quarters.”
Hideyuki Ishiguro, Chief Strategist at Nomura Asset Management, said chip stocks are currently under pressure partly due to concerns over memory supply and demand, and profit taking from leveraged ETF funds. He pointed out that short-term prices are more driven by supply-demand dynamics and sentiment, but over the medium to long term, chip manufacturers are still expected to benefit from profit growth and free cash flow expansion fueled by artificial intelligence .
As investors reassess the next stage of the artificial intelligence trade, they are increasingly shifting out of technology stocks into other industries.
KCM Trade Chief Market Analyst Tim Waterer said, “The market is adjusting the competitive landscape for valuations. After semiconductors stole the spotlight for months, investors are now diversifying their bets into other higher-value sectors, dampening the previous optimism for high-beta tech stocks.” He said this rotation could last for some time, until the elevated valuations of semiconductor companies better align with those of the rest of the market.
